slides.title: Negative Exponents with Variable Bases
slides.note: Post the learning target. Say the 'today' line and nothing else yet.

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.sub: On your own. Four minutes. No notes.
slides.note: Q2 and Q4 together are the lesson: a negative exponent asks for a reciprocal. Q2 is the numerical version from 3.04; today the same law is applied to x. A student with −25 on Q2 will write −x² today, and that is the board to find early.

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.note: Reveal. Ask for the band each question came from only if time allows.

slides.title: Notes
slides.note:
The 3.04 pattern table again, with x in place of 2: each entry is the previous one divided by x. After x⁰ = 1 the next division gives 1/x, then 1/x², then 1/x³. Students fill the last three cells before the rule is written. The state guide asks for this table (its task 2, with base m: m⁻⁵ to m⁵, 'why is m⁰ = 1') and for a written contrast of x³ and x⁻³ — that contrast is whiteboard 9.
OFF: 'x⁻³ is one over x³. It is a reciprocal. It is not negative, and it is not −3x.'

slides.title: Notes
slides.note:
Each factor with a negative exponent moves across the bar on its own and its exponent turns positive. The coefficient does NOT move unless it has the negative exponent: 3x⁻² is 3 over x², not 1 over 3x². That is today's leading misconception and it is on whiteboard 3 and 6. The guide's item y⁻³z⁻⁴ = 1/(y³z⁴) is the second line.
OFF: 'Only the factor wearing the negative exponent moves. Everything else stays put.'

slides.title: Notes
slides.note: Product and quotient laws are unchanged; the exponents are integers now, so the sums and differences can land below zero. The last step is always to write the answer with positive exponents. x⁴ · x⁻⁶ is x⁻², which is 1/x². m³/m⁷ is m⁻⁴, which is 1/m⁴ — and ask the class to check it by cancelling three m's from seven.

slides.title: Example 1
slides.note: SPOKEN ONLY. Same regrouping as yesterday: coefficients, x's, y's. Ask what −3 + 5 is and what 2 + (−4) is before anyone writes — the whole example is integer addition.

slides.title: Example 1
slides.note: Add the exponents of each variable, then move the y⁻² down. A board with 12x²y⁻² stopped one step early; a board with 12x⁻⁸y⁶ subtracted where it should have added; a board with x²/(12y²) moved the coefficient down too.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.
slides.note: Catches the coefficient-mover (a³/(4b²)) and the sign-dropper (4a⁷b⁴). 4a³/b² is right.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.note: Reveal; name what a wrong board most likely did (see the note above).

slides.title: Example 2
slides.sub: Several laws in one expression — the state guide's item.
slides.note: SPOKEN ONLY. Three laws: power of a quotient, power of a product (the 4 is raised), and the negative exponent. Ask which to do first (the outside exponent) and what happens to the 4.

slides.title: Example 2
slides.note: Raise every factor to the 5th: a¹⁵ on top, 4⁵ = 1,024 and b⁻³⁵ on the bottom. Then b⁻³⁵ moves up. The B1G-M's own description of the result: 'only two exponents, no negatives'. A board with 20 instead of 1,024 multiplied 4 by 5; a board with a¹⁵/(1,024b³⁵) never moved the b.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.
slides.note: Catches the un-raised coefficient (x⁶y⁶/3) and the b-that-did-not-move (x⁶/(27y⁶)). x⁶y⁶/27 is right.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.note: Reveal; name what a wrong board most likely did (see the note above).

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 1 of 9
slides.note: The law, plain, with a letter. A board with −x⁴ made the exponent's sign the sign of the expression; a board with −4x multiplied.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 1 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 2 of 9
slides.note: The second form. A board with 1/y⁵ made the exponent positive without moving the power.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 2 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 3 of 9
slides.note: Ruling 22's board: the model's length is there to be read past. The coefficient stays put. A board with 1/(3x²) moved the 3 as well — today's leading error, and the one to name at the board.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 3 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 4 of 9
slides.note: The state guide's own item. A board with 1/(yz)⁷ or 1/(yz⁷) combined unlike bases.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 4 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 5 of 9
slides.note: Diagnostic. D is the board that says Notes I did not land — go back to the table and divide 1 by x twice, out loud.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 5 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 6 of 9
slides.note: Diagnostic for two laws at once. B and D are the two coefficient errors; C is the exponent error.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 6 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 7 of 9
slides.note: Subtraction landing below zero. A board with m⁴ subtracted the wrong way; a board with m⁻⁴ stopped one step early. Cancelling three m's from seven confirms the answer.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 7 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 8 of 9
slides.note: Working backwards across zero. A board with −3 added 2 and −5; a board with −7 has the sign wrong. −5 + 7 = 2.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 8 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 9 of 9
slides.sub: Take your time. Boards up when you have written it.
slides.note: Written. The state guide's new task for this benchmark, done as a written contrast. Full credit: the word reciprocal (or '1 over x³') and both values. A student who writes −8 for x⁻³ has the day's misconception; one who writes 'opposites' has the 3.04 confusion of opposite with reciprocal.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 9 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Independent Set
slides.sub: Six questions. On your own, in silence.
slides.note: Hand out the Independent Set. Silent work. Circulate and mark what you see; do not teach. Whatever is not finished goes home.

slides.title: IXL
slides.note: IXL: every listed skill is required, SmartScore 67. Due at the start of the next class.
